lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you learnt to ask first, before sharing a photo of someone. What is the respectful answer to 'no'? (Accept it.) Today: respectful relationships online, and getting help with pressure.

Respect online is the same as face to face: kind words, asking first, and accepting no. A screen can make people forget that a real person reads every message. Before you post, think: is it true, kind and needed?

picture.name: Ana
messages: Can I post the photo of us at the park?
Not that one, I had my eyes shut!
No problem, I'll use the other one.

lesson.text: Healthy friendships online have trust and kindness, and respect your time and privacy. Warning signs of control: checking where you are, and anger if you don't reply at once. Asking for passwords, or deciding who you can talk to, are warnings too.
Consent means a free yes. Ask before posting a photo of someone, and take it down if they ask. Never forward something private. A no can't be changed by pushing, and a yes can be taken back.

Never send nude or nearly nude pictures, and never ask anyone for one. In UK law it is a crime to make, keep or share such a picture of anyone under 18, even of yourself. The law is there to protect you.

picture.name: unknown
messages: You're so mature for your age.
Send me a photo of you.

lesson.text: It is never your fault if someone pressures you or shares a picture. Don't reply, keep the evidence, block, report and tell a trusted adult. Childline's Report Remove helps take a picture down. CEOP is for adults who pressure young people.

Your digital footprint is everything you post, like and share: it can last and be copied. Be an upstander, not a bystander: don't join in with unkindness, support the person, and report hateful posts.

Try it in the world: check your privacy settings with a grown-up. In LIFE, Calm Corner practises dealing with unkind messages, and the Connections Book shows how to protect your good name online. Next: chance and spending.

exercises.prompt: Respect online means the same kind words and asking first as face to face.
exercises.hint: Is a person behind a screen still a real person?
exercises.explain: True: a real person reads every message, so the same respect applies online.

exercises.prompt: Before posting a group photo, what should you do?
exercises.hint: Who has a say over a photo of them?
exercises.explain: Everyone in a photo has a right to say yes or no before it is posted.

exercises.prompt: A healthy friendship, or a warning sign?
items: gets angry if you see other friends
checks where you are all the time
accepts it when you say no
exercises.hint: Does it respect your choices, or try to control them?
exercises.explain: Healthy: accepting no, giving time. Warning signs: asking for passwords, anger about friends, checking up.

exercises.prompt: In the chat, what did Ana do well?

picture.name: Ana
messages: Can I post the photo of us at the park?
Not that one, I had my eyes shut!
No problem, I'll use the other one.

choices: asked first and accepted the answer
argued until she got her way
exercises.explain: Ana asked before posting and happily chose another photo when the answer was no.

exercises.prompt: Someone keeps sending you unkind messages. Put the steps in order.
exercises.hint: Stop it growing, save the proof, stop them, report them, get help.
exercises.explain: Don't reply, keep the evidence, block, report, and tell a trusted adult.

exercises.prompt: Which message in this chat is the biggest warning sign?

picture.name: unknown
messages: You're so mature for your age.
Send me a photo of you.

exercises.hint: Read the marked message, and the one about secrets.
exercises.explain: Asking for photos and secrecy from a stranger are warning signs: stop, don't send anything, tell an adult.

exercises.prompt: If a private picture is shared, the person in it is to blame.
exercises.hint: Who chose to share it without permission?
exercises.explain: False: it is never the fault of the person in the picture. The people who shared it did wrong.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
matches: a free yes, which can change
exercises.hint: Think of the lesson's words about choices, traces and what people do.
exercises.explain: Consent: a free yes. Footprint: all you post. Upstander: helps. Bystander: only watches.

exercises.prompt: A classmate's private picture is going round a group chat. What should you do?
choices: don't forward it, and tell a trusted adult
exercises.hint: Which choice stops the harm spreading?
exercises.explain: Never forward it; telling a trusted adult gets it stopped and the person supported.

exercises.prompt: UK law protects everyone under what age from nude pictures being made, kept or shared?
exercises.hint: It is the same age as being an adult in the UK.
exercises.explain: Under 18: it is a crime to make, keep or share such a picture of anyone under 18.

items: messages the person to check they're OK
exercises.hint: Who helps, and who just watches or joins in?
exercises.explain: Upstanders report, check in and tell; bystanders scroll past or join in.

exercises.prompt: Someone threatens to share a picture of you unless you send more. What do you do?
choices: send nothing; tell an adult; report to CEOP
exercises.hint: Giving in never stops this. Who can step in?
exercises.explain: Send nothing more, keep the evidence, tell a trusted adult and report to CEOP: adults who pressure young people break the law.

exercises.prompt: A 'yes' to posting a photo can be taken back later.
exercises.hint: Is consent a free choice that can change?
exercises.explain: True: consent can be taken back, so take the photo down if your friend asks.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best check before posting something about someone else?
choices: is it true, kind and needed?
will it get lots of likes?
exercises.hint: Think about the person it is about.
exercises.explain: Asking whether a post is true, kind and needed protects other people and your own digital footprint.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of helping get a picture taken down in order.
items: stay calm: it's not your fault
exercises.hint: Feelings first, then a grown-up, then the tools.
exercises.explain: Remember it is not your fault, tell a trusted adult, use Report Remove, then block and report.
